system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2145-10-11 14:28:00 to 2145-10-12 18:54:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of recurrent pulmonary emboli, chronic pain, COPD, and anticoagulation on Lovenox was admitted for worsening bilateral pleuritic chest pain and new right bicep pain. He was concerned about a new clot but showed no clinical signs of acute cardiopulmonary deterioration. A chest X-ray revealed no acute process, and a right upper extremity ultrasound showed no DVT. Pain was managed with a short-term increase in oxycodone from 5mg to 10mg every 4 hours, with plans to taper back to baseline. Anxiety was addressed with hydroxyzine and non-pharmacologic strategies. His condition stabilized, pain improved, and he was discharged home with instructions to continue Lovenox, taper oxycodone over 8 days, and follow up with pain management. No new clots were diagnosed during this admission.
problems: Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Diverticulitis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)

Dear Mr. ___,

___. You were admitted for diarrhea, abdominal pain,

___. You will be discharged on several days of pain 
medications for your chronic pain. It is important that you 
followup with a primary care physician and ___ pain clinic to 
manage your chronic pain.

you continue care with your primary care physician at ___,

he has all the necessary information. We also tried to establish 
care here with Dr. ___ you did not desire this option. 
Because of your prior narcotics violations within our system, we 
are unable at this time to set you up with another primary care 
physician ___.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with history of multiple thromboses presenting
with abdominal pain and chest pain, off anticoagulations for five days.  Rule
out pulmonary embolism or arterial thrombus.

COMPARISONS:  Multiple prior CTs, most recently CT chest ___ and
CT abdomen and pelvis of ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained from the thoracic inlet to the upper
abdomen after administration of 120 cc of IV Omnipaque contrast timed for
opacification of the thoracic aorta.  Images were subsequently acquired
through the abdomen and pelvis.  An additional arterial phase sequence was
obtained through the abdominal aorta after administration of additional IV
contrast.

FINDINGS:

CHEST CTA:  The great vessels are normal caliber.  The thoracic aorta is
normal without aneurysm or dissection.  The main, lobar, segmental, and
proximal subsegmental pulmonary arteries are opacified without filling defect.
The previously identified pulmonary emboli are no longer visualized.

CHEST:  

No axillary, mediastinal, or hilar lymphadenopathy.  The heart is normal size.
No pericardial effusion.  4-mm right lower lobe nodule is similar to ___ but minimally enlarged since ___.  No focal consolidation,
pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or pneumomediastinum.  Airways are patent to
subsegmental levels.  The esophagus is normal.  

ABDOMEN:

The liver, gallbladder, intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts, pancreas, and
adrenal glands are normal.  The spleen is absent.  A 1.3-cm splenule is noted.
A 2.0-cm cystic lesion in the lower pole of the left kidney is of intermediate
density, and is enlarged since ___, previously partially
characterized on ultrasound as a complex cyst.  Cortical defects of the right
kidney are similar to prior.  The kidneys enhance symmetrically and excrete
contrast promptly.  The ureters are normal in course and caliber.

The stomach is normal.  The small and large bowel have a normal course and
caliber.

The abdominal aorta is unremarkable without aneurysm or dissection.  No
filling defect is present within the abdominal aorta.  The celiac axis has
conventional anatomy.  The splenic artery is not opacified.  The portal veins
are patent.

An infrarenal IVC filter appears in similar position to prior, but one of the
prongs of the IVC filter is now oriented superiorly and abuts the IVC wall. 
No active extravasation of contrast or large adjacent hematoma.  A
non-obstructing thrombus extends from the superior aspect of the IVC filter
and appears new since ___.

No retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  No free abdominal fluid or
pneumoperitoneum.  The patient is status post ventral hernia repair.  A right
fat-containing Spigelian hernia (2B:98) is similar to prior.

The bladder and terminal ureters are normal.  The prostate gland and seminal
vesicles are normal.  No pelvic sidewall or inguinal lymphadenopathy.  No free
pelvic fluid.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  No focal lytic or sclerotic lesion concerning for
malignancy.  Multilevel thoracolumbar spine degenerative changes are present.

IMPRESSION:  

1.  New non-occlusive IVC thrombus extending superiorly from the infrarenal
IVC filter.  A prong of the IVC filter is newly oriented superiorly and abuts
the wall of the IVC.  No active extravasation of contrast or adjacent
hematoma.

2.  No pulmonary embolus visualized.  Previously seen pulmonary emboli no
longer present.

3.  2.0 cm intermediate density left lower pole renal cyst, previously
characterized on US as a complex cyst, has enlarged since ___.  Given

4.  4-mm right lower lobe pulmonary nodule, stable since ___, but
increased since ___.  Follow-up suggested in 6 months.

5.  Right fat-containing Spigelian hernia, similar to prior.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the chest pain started a couple days ago. It’s in the lower left side, same spot as my last pulmonary embolism. Hurts worse when I breathe or press on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like pleuritic pain. Any shortness of breath, cough, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had some shortness of breath and a cough. I always have a little blood in my sputum—hemoptysis—but it hasn’t changed. And I’ve had chills and low-grade fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the abdominal pain and diarrhea—when did those start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diarrhea started about three days ago—yellowish, loose stools, four times a day. No blood. Then the next day, I got pain in the lower left abdomen. Feels like when I had diverticulitis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And have you been taking your Lovenox regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ran out five days ago. I called my PCP, but got voicemail. I couldn’t get a refill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Being off anticoagulation could explain some of this. We’ve ordered a CT scan to check for clots. We’ll also run blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—no pulmonary embolism. But we did see something concerning: a new blood clot near your IVC filter. It’s not blocking flow, but it’s new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Could it move?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The filter caught it, which is exactly what it’s supposed to do. There’s no sign it’s causing damage or leaking. Vascular surgery reviewed it and said no surgery is needed. But it likely formed because you were off Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just restart the Lovenox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve already restarted it. You’ll need to stay on it indefinitely. We’re also sending a prescription to your pharmacy for a month’s supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the chest pain? Is it from the clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain isn’t from a new PE. Your heart tests are normal—no heart attack. The pain is likely musculoskeletal, maybe costochondritis. It’s reproducible when I press here, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that’s exactly where it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That supports it being a chest wall issue. We’ll manage it with acetaminophen and a short course of oxycodone if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something now? It’s been really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I can give you 5 mg of oxycodone now. But we need to be careful—your history includes substance use, and we want to avoid over-reliance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but the pain is real. I’m not trying to misuse anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. We’ll treat your pain appropriately. We’re also giving hydroxyzine for anxiety, which can make pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now, about two hours after the medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still there. Can I have another dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet—it’s only been two hours. The oxycodone is every four hours as needed. Let’s try breathing exercises and repositioning. We can reassess in two hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I had an accident—fecal incontinence earlier. I’m embarrassed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay, Mr. ___. It happens, especially with diarrhea. We’ve noted it. Your stools are softening, which is a good sign. The diarrhea seems mild—likely viral. No antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want this to stop. And I’m worried about the clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The clot is stable. The filter did its job. The key is staying on Lovenox. We’re setting you up with your PCP to manage refills so this doesn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—kidneys, liver, and electrolytes are fine. No signs of infection. We’re planning to discharge you today if you’re feeling okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? What about the IVC filter? Shouldn’t someone check it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery reviewed it. The filter shifted slightly but isn’t piercing the vein. No intervention needed. But you must follow up with your doctor to monitor it long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed a few appointments. I’ll try to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already called your pharmacy—your Lovenox is ready. We’re also faxing your PCP with the details. You need to see them within a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain meds when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with 20 tablets of oxycodone 5 mg—take one every six hours only if needed. Don’t exceed that. Continue acetaminophen as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety? I still can’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking trazodone and hydroxyzine at night. Avoid screens before bed. If it continues, talk to your PCP about adjusting the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Remember: take Lovenox every day, follow up with your PCP, and keep your pain clinic appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll do my best to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Call if you have chest pain that worsens, shortness of breath, or any bleeding. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—how are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Chest pain is better, stomach feels calmer. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—should I worry about the kidney cyst they saw on the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been there and is stable. They recommend an MRI in a few months to check it. Mention it at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. Thanks for answering all my questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Stay safe, and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—everything looks good. You’re officially discharged. Go home, rest, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help. I’ll stay on my meds and make that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of recurrent venous thromboembolism, IVC filter placement, chronic pain, and non-adherence to anticoagulation presented with pleuritic chest pain, LLQ abdominal pain, and mild diarrhea after running out of Lovenox five days prior. Imaging revealed a new non-occlusive thrombus at the IVC filter site, which had shifted but not penetrated the vessel wall. No pulmonary embolism or acute cardiac issue was found. The chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, and diarrhea was likely viral. He was restarted on Lovenox, managed for pain and anxiety, and discharged home with a short course of oxycodone, clear instructions on anticoagulation adherence, and follow-up plans with his PCP and pain clinic.
